statement: Centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE) is defined as training that may use centrally shared information (e.g. all agents' observation histories or the full state) to update agent policies, while each agent's deployed policy is conditioned only on its own local observation history, so it can be executed independently; the value function used during training is no longer needed at execution time.
evidence_type: textbook exposition
conditions: applies when the application scenario allows privileged information to be shared only during training, not at deployment
limits: none stated in this passage

statement: In independent learning, each agent treats the other agents as part of a non-stationary component of the environment rather than modeling them explicitly; as other agents' policies change, the transition, observation, and reward functions perceived by each individual agent change too, which the authors state can lead to unstable learning and poor convergence, despite independent learning often performing well in practice.
evidence_type: textbook exposition
conditions: applies to fully decentralized training and execution where agents cannot or do not model other agents
limits: the authors note this is a known challenge, not a proof of failure in all cases; independent learning 'often performs well in practice'

statement: Off-policy independent learning with a replay buffer (e.g. IDQN) can retain stale experience: as illustrated by a chess example where agent 2 learns to counter agent 1's opening, agent 1's replay buffer continues to hold now-outdated transitions that overstate the old opening's value, which can delay agent 1 from abandoning the countered strategy.
evidence_type: worked example
conditions: applies to off-policy algorithms using a replay buffer under concurrent multi-agent learning
limits: illustrative example, not an empirical measurement; mitigations discussed include smaller buffers, importance-sampling reweighting (Foerster et al. 2017), hysteretic Q-learning, and leniency

statement: On-policy independent algorithms such as REINFORCE are stated to be less susceptible to the replay-buffer staleness problem than off-policy algorithms like IDQN, because they always learn from experience generated under the most recent (current) policies of the other agents.
evidence_type: textbook exposition
conditions: applies to on-policy independent policy-gradient methods (REINFORCE, A2C, PPO) versus off-policy value-based methods with replay buffers
limits: stated as a qualitative advantage, not quantified

statement: IDQN (Algorithm 17) gives each agent i its own action-value network Q(.;theta_i), its own target network, and its own replay buffer D_i; each agent's DQN loss (Eq. 9.1) is computed only from that agent's own local observation history, action, and reward, with no information sharing between agents at training or execution time, though all agents' losses are optimized simultaneously.
evidence_type: textbook exposition with algorithm pseudocode
conditions: fully decentralized training and execution
limits: none stated beyond the general independent-learning caveats

statement: Under CTDE, the actor network is conditioned only on agent i's local observation history h_i^t to preserve decentralized execution, while the critic (discarded after training) may be conditioned on any additional information beyond the agent's own history and action, including other agents' observation histories or the full environment state, forming a vector z; the critic's value loss (Eq. 9.10) uses this z as part of its input.
evidence_type: textbook exposition
conditions: CTDE paradigm; critic is unused after training completes
limits: chunk B01-C0058 is flagged equation_text_unreliable, so exact operator glyphs in Eq. 9.10 should be checked against the source page

statement: Lyu et al. (2023), as reported by the authors, show that a centralized critic should at minimum be conditioned on the agent's own observation history (otherwise it may be biased and unable to infer the policy it evaluates), and that additional centralized information can introduce higher variance into the policy gradient during training without improving theoretical convergence guarantees, though the authors note this theoretical result relies on an assumption -- convergence of critics to true value functions under current policies -- that often does not hold in deep-learning practice, and empirically added information sometimes still helps avoid local optima.
evidence_type: theoretical analysis cited from an external paper, reported without proof in this chunk
conditions: theoretical claim assumes critic convergence to true value functions under all agents' current policies
limits: authors explicitly state this theoretical assumption often fails in deep RL practice, and cite Lowe et al. 2017 and Papoudakis et al. 2021 as empirical counterpoints where extra information still helps

statement: Difference rewards (Eq. 9.14) approximate agent i's contribution to a common reward as the difference between the actual received reward and the reward agent i would have received under a chosen default action, holding other agents' actions fixed; the aristocrat utility (Eq. 9.15) avoids needing a default action by instead subtracting the expected reward agent i would receive under its current policy.
evidence_type: textbook exposition
conditions: applies in common-reward games; computing exact difference rewards requires access to the reward function (or a learned model of it) and, for the non-aristocrat form, a chosen default action
limits: authors note it is often unclear how to select a default action, and computing R_i(s,<default,a_{-i}>) requires reward-function access

statement: COMA's counterfactual baseline (Eq. 9.16) computes the advantage of agent i's chosen action by subtracting, from the centralized action-value estimate, the expectation over agent i's own policy of the same centralized action-value with other agents' actions a_{-i} held fixed; the text states this baseline does not change the multi-agent policy gradient (Eq. 9.9) in expectation.
evidence_type: stated result, proof not reproduced in this chunk
conditions: requires a trained centralized action-value critic Q(h_i, z, a; theta) conditioned on all agents' actions
limits: chunk B01-C0059 flagged equation_text_unreliable; exact operator glyphs in Eq. 9.16 should be checked against the source page

statement: Despite its unbiased-in-expectation motivation, COMA is reported to empirically suffer from high variance in its counterfactual baseline (citing Kuba et al. 2021) and inconsistent value estimates (citing Vasilev et al. 2021), which the authors state 'result in unstable training that can lead to poor performance' (citing Papoudakis et al. 2021).
evidence_type: authors' synthesis of cited empirical findings
conditions: reported as a general property of COMA across the cited studies, not a specific reproduced experiment in this book
limits: the book does not reproduce the underlying experiments in this range; this is a secondhand synthesis

statement: A game is defined as no-conflict (Eq. 9.17) if all agents share the same argmax joint policy over their expected returns, i.e. they agree on the single most-preferred outcome even if they disagree on lower-ranked outcomes; the Stag Hunt is given as a no-conflict example where agents agree (A,A) is best but disagree on the second-best outcome, and any common-reward game is stated to always be no-conflict.

evidence_type: textbook exposition with a worked matrix-game example
conditions: definition applies to normal-form/matrix games as presented; extended informally to common-reward stochastic games via the Climbing game example
limits: none stated

statement: In the Climbing matrix game and in a penalized cooperative level-based-foraging task, centralized A2C is reported to converge to a suboptimal, risk-averse equilibrium (avoiding the penalty by never attempting the cooperative action), while Pareto actor-critic (Pareto-AC), which optimistically assumes other agents best-respond to maximize agent i's return, is reported to converge to the Pareto-optimal equilibrium in both tasks.
section: 9.5 Value Decomposition in Common-Reward Games (reporting Section 9.4.5 experiments)
evidence_type: empirical figure reproduced from cited paper (Christianos, Papoudakis, and Albrecht 2023), reported by the textbook authors
conditions: Climbing matrix game and a specific penalized level-based-foraging cooperative-collection task with a fixed 5x5 grid and two agents
limits: fixed small-scale tasks (one matrix game, one 2-agent grid task); not claimed to generalize beyond these settings

statement: The text states that Pareto-AC's practical computation of the best-response set pi+_{-i} via an argmax over other agents' joint actions (Eq. 9.21) 'has unattractive scaling properties as the number of agents increases' and that finding tractable approximations for this iteration 'remains unresolved' -- the book does not claim Pareto-AC scales to large or variable agent counts.
section: 9.4.5 Equilibrium Selection with Centralized Action-Value Critics
evidence_type: authors' stated limitation
conditions: applies to the joint-action-value-function-based computation of pi+_{-i} in Pareto-AC
limits: explicitly an open/unresolved problem per the text; not evidence Pareto-AC works for large N

statement: The individual-global-max (IGM) property (Eq. 9.25) requires that, for all full histories, a joint action is a greedy action of the decomposed centralized action-value function if and only if each agent's component action is a greedy action of that agent's own individual utility function; the authors note that in some environments, particularly under partial observability, no decomposition satisfying IGM may exist because individual utilities can lack the information to discriminate joint histories with different true action values.
evidence_type: textbook exposition of a formal definition
conditions: defined over full histories h-hat with joint-observation history h = sigma(h-hat), individual histories h_i = sigma_i(h-hat), and centralized information z
limits: existence of an IGM-satisfying decomposition is not guaranteed for all environments per the authors' own caveat

statement: The book proves in both directions that any linear decomposition of the centralized action-value function -- where the function equals the sum of per-agent utility functions Q(h_i, a_i; theta_i) (Eq. 9.26-9.30) -- satisfies the IGM property (Eq. 9.25); this linear decomposition defines the value decomposition networks (VDN) algorithm (Sunehag et al. 2018).
evidence_type: stated theorem with full proof
conditions: assumes the common reward decomposes as a sum of per-agent utilities (Eq. 9.26)
limits: chunk B01-C0060/B01-C0061 flagged equation_text_unreliable; exact operator glyphs in the proof (Eq. 9.31-9.42) should be checked against the source pages

statement: VDN (Algorithm 21) trains per-agent utility networks Q(h_i, a_i; theta_i), summed to form a single centralized action-value estimate, using one shared replay buffer that stores joint transitions (h^t, a^t, r^t, h^{t+1}) and a shared training loss (Eq. 9.43) optimized jointly across all agents; at execution, each agent selects actions greedily with respect to only its own individual utility function, requiring no communication.
evidence_type: textbook exposition with algorithm pseudocode
conditions: common-reward (shared-reward) games
limits: the text notes no constraints are imposed on individual utility functions; only shared rewards are used during optimization

statement: QMIX's monotonicity condition (Eq. 9.46) -- the partial derivative of the centralized action-value function with respect to every agent's utility is strictly positive -- is proved sufficient for the IGM property in both directions. A footnote gives the non-strict version (>= 0, Eq. 9.59) used in the original QMIX paper (Rashid et al. 2018) and constructs an explicit two-agent counterexample (Eq. 9.60-9.62) showing that without strict positivity the '<=' direction of IGM equivalence fails.
evidence_type: stated theorem with full proof plus a footnote counterexample
conditions: mixing network f_mix must have (strictly) positive weights with respect to the utility inputs; bias vectors are unconstrained
limits: the footnote explicitly documents that the weaker non-strict condition used in the original QMIX paper does not by itself guarantee the full IGM equivalence

statement: The set of centralized action-value functions representable by QMIX's monotonic decomposition is a strict superset of those representable by VDN's linear decomposition: any linear decomposition is monotonic, but a monotonic decomposition with positive per-agent weights alpha_i(h) that vary by joint-observation history (Eq. 9.64) is not linear unless those weights are constant, and VDN can only represent equal weighting (alpha_i = 1 for all agents and histories).
evidence_type: textbook exposition with a worked counterexample
conditions: compares the representable function classes of VDN (linear) and QMIX (monotonic)
limits: none stated

statement: In the Climbing matrix game, which has no simple linear or monotonic decomposition matching the true reward table, both VDN (converging to joint action (C,C), reward +5) and QMIX (converging to (C,B), reward +6) fail to recover the true optimal joint action (A,A), reward +11, and both learn inaccurate value-function decompositions.
evidence_type: empirical figure reproduced in the textbook's own experiments
conditions: single 3x3 matrix game (Climbing game), trained until convergence per the authors' stated experimental protocol (footnote 12, feedforward networks, Adam optimizer, learning rate 3e-4, up to 20,000 steps)
limits: single matrix-game demonstration, not a broad benchmark; illustrates a known failure mode rather than a general bound

statement: In a shared-reward, two-agent, 8x8-grid level-based-foraging environment (three items, randomized levels/positions, episodes up to 25 steps), QMIX is reported to significantly outperform both VDN and IDQN in average evaluation return, learning speed, and variance across five runs with different random seeds over two million environment steps; VDN outperforms IDQN but shows notably higher variance across runs than QMIX.
evidence_type: empirical figure from the textbook's own experiments, 5 seeds
conditions: two-agent, 8x8 level-based foraging, shared reward, fixed network sizes (two-layer, 64-hidden-unit utility networks; 32-hidden-unit QMIX mixing network), epsilon-greedy exploration annealed 1 to 0.05
limits: fixed agent count (2); single environment configuration; 5-seed evaluation only

statement: Son et al. (2019)'s necessary-and-sufficient conditions for the IGM property (Eq. 9.67-9.69) combine three jointly-optimized components: a linear sum of per-agent individual utility functions, an unrestricted (non-decomposed) centralized action-value function Q(h,z,a;theta_q), and a centralized correction utility V(h,z;theta_v); the text states these conditions are also necessary under an affine transformation of the individual utilities (Eq. 9.70, with positive scale alpha_i and arbitrary offset beta_i).

statement: The text explicitly states that QTRAN's practical training procedure only minimizes soft regularization losses (Eq. 9.72 and 9.74) that reach their minimum when the IGM conditions of Eq. 9.67/9.69 are satisfied, and that consequently 'these properties are only satisfied asymptotically and not throughout the entire training process' -- the book does not claim QTRAN maintains the IGM guarantee at arbitrary points during training, only that regularization pushes toward it.

statement: Every value-decomposition experiment reported in this range (matrix games with 2 or 3 fixed actions per agent, and the level-based-foraging comparisons) uses a fixed, small agent count (2 or 3 agents) within a single training run per task; the book does not test or claim that a learned linear (VDN), monotonic (QMIX), or QTRAN-style decomposition continues to satisfy IGM, or continues to perform well, when the number of agents varies from what it was trained with. Held-out or scaled agent-count evaluation is not reported in Sections 9.4-9.5.

statement: The IGM property's requirement that per-agent greedy actions computed from local utilities compose exactly into the joint-greedy action of a shared centralized value function (Eq. 9.25), and QMIX's concrete algebraic sufficient condition for it (strict positive partial derivative of the centralized value with respect to each agent's utility, Eq. 9.46), are a natural formal target for any HMASD component that wants a per-agent (or per-skill) greedy selection to remain consistent with a team-level objective as the number of agents N changes; this book's proofs and counterexamples (e.g. the non-strict-monotonicity failure in footnote 9, p. 280-281) are candidate correctness checks for such a mixer, not evidence that HMASD itself satisfies them.
evidence_type: curator's prospective connection between book content and HMASD design questions
conditions: prospective only; no HMASD code or result is implied by the book's proofs
limits: this is a curator-authored connection, not a claim the book itself makes about HMASD or any variable-N MARL algorithm
